slides.title: Shipping while users keep working
points: A zero-downtime deploy replaces the running version without failed requests or a maintenance page.
It needs cooperation from the load balancer, the app and the database.

slides.title: Drain, roll, migrate safely
points: Rolling update: replace instances a few at a time; each new one takes traffic only when its readiness check passes.
Graceful shutdown: an old instance stops taking new requests, finishes the ones in flight, then exits.
Database changes use expand and contract, so old and new code both work during the rollout.
Blue-green or canary for risky releases, with a fast rollback.

slides.title: More steps, no outages
points: Running two versions side by side means the API and schema must be compatible both ways.
Long-lived connections (WebSockets) need draining time and client reconnects.
Volume-backed services that can't run two copies at once can't overlap deploys; their start-up time is downtime, so make it short.

slides.title: What it looks like
points: Health endpoints that report ready only after warm-up.
SIGTERM handled: stop accepting, finish, exit within the grace period.
Deploy dashboards showing error rate by version during the rollout.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: When a whole cloud region goes dark
points: Cloud regions occasionally fail for hours. Surviving that means running, or being able to run quickly, somewhere else.
The design depends on how long the business can be down and how much data it can lose.

slides.title: Standby to active-active
points: Backup and restore: data copied to another region; rebuild there when needed (hours).
Warm standby: a scaled-down copy running in a second region, data replicated, scaled up on failover (minutes).
Active-active: both regions serve traffic; routing moves users away from the failed one (seconds), with data-consistency work.
DNS or global load balancers steer traffic between regions using health checks.

slides.title: Cost and complexity
points: Each step up roughly doubles the infrastructure and the testing.
Cross-region replication adds latency; synchronous replication slows every write.
Hidden single-region dependencies (an identity provider, a queue) break the plan.

slides.title: What it looks like
points: A dependency map checked for single-region pieces.
Failover drills at least yearly, with the clock running.
A decision rule for when to fail over, so nobody hesitates during an incident.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Paying for what you use
points: Cloud bills grow quietly: oversized machines, idle environments, forgotten storage, data transfer.
Cutting them is ongoing engineering work, not a one-off.

slides.title: See, shrink, commit
points: See: tag every resource with team and service; report cost per team weekly.
Shrink: right-size instances, delete idle resources, turn off non-production at night, set storage lifecycle rules.
Commit: savings plans or reserved capacity for steady load; spot for interruptible work.
Architect: cache to cut repeated work, keep data and compute in the same region to avoid transfer charges.

slides.title: Savings against speed and safety
points: Commitments save money and lock you in for a year or three.
Spot instances save a lot and can vanish with two minutes' notice.
Cuts that remove reliability headroom cost more in the next incident.

slides.title: What it looks like
points: Budgets and anomaly alerts per account.
Cost shown next to performance in service reviews.
A quarterly clean-up of snapshots, logs and unused environments.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Something's broken; find it, out loud
points: You're given a scenario ('the website is slow', 'a server is unreachable') and asked how you'd investigate, often on a live machine.
They're scoring method: hypotheses, the cheapest checks first, and narrowing down.

slides.title: A method
points: Clarify: what changed, since when, who's affected, how bad?
Work the layers: DNS, network, load balancer, host (CPU, memory, disk), process, application logs, dependencies.
Use measurements, not guesses: top, df, free, ss, curl -v, logs.
Mitigate first if users are hurting; root-cause after.

slides.title: Methodical, not random
points: Jumping to a favourite cause wastes time when it's wrong.
Saying 'I'd check X because Y' scores better than silently typing.
Knowing when to escalate or roll back is part of the answer.

slides.title: How to prepare
points: Practise on a VM: break things on purpose and fix them.
Learn the ten commands you'd reach for first, and what each tells you.
Prepare a real incident story with your role in it.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Design the platform for a service
points: You're asked to design infrastructure for something specific: a web app expecting rapid growth, a data pipeline, a multi-tenant SaaS.
They're scoring reliability, security, cost and operability, not cloud trivia.

slides.title: Cover the layers
points: Requirements: traffic, data size, availability target, compliance.
Compute, networking, data stores, caching, and how traffic flows between them.
Deploys, observability, secrets, access, backups and DR.
Cost at the expected scale, and what changes at ten times that.

slides.title: Justify every box
points: Kubernetes for a single small app is hard to justify; say why or why not.
Managed services save effort; mention the lock-in honestly.
Over-designing for a scale that isn't coming costs money and time.

slides.title: How to prepare
points: Practise three designs end to end, with a rough cost.
Draw network boundaries (public, private) clearly.
End with what you'd monitor and how you'd fail over.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: 'You're paged at 3 a.m.; what do you do?'
points: On-call interviews walk through a simulated incident to see how you act under pressure.
They're scoring calm prioritisation, communication and safe actions.

slides.title: Acknowledge, assess, mitigate, communicate
points: Acknowledge the page and check the alert's dashboard and runbook.
Assess impact: who's affected and how badly; declare an incident if needed.
Mitigate with the safest effective action (roll back, fail over, scale up).
Communicate early and regularly; hand over cleanly; write up afterwards.

slides.title: Act, but carefully
points: Risky fixes at 3 a.m. can make things worse; prefer reversible actions.
Calling for help early is a strength, not a weakness.
Silence during an incident worries everyone; short updates help.

slides.title: How to prepare
points: Walk through a past incident: your timeline and decisions.
Know what a good runbook contains.
Practise saying what you'd communicate, and to whom.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

newQuestions.stem: Every deploy causes a burst of 502 errors as old instances shut down. What's usually missing?
choices: Graceful shutdown: on SIGTERM, stop taking new requests, finish in-flight ones, and let the load balancer deregister the instance first
why: Requests are cut off mid-flight when an instance exits abruptly.
Memory isn't the cause.
That makes detection slower.
That makes each deploy bigger and riskier.

newQuestions.stem: During a failover drill, the second region's app servers start, but every sign-in fails. What's the likely cause?
choices: A hidden single-region dependency, such as the sign-in service or its secrets living only in the failed region
why: Drills exist to find dependencies like this before a real outage.
Size wouldn't fail every sign-in.
Not a cause of failed sign-ins.
All at once? No.

newQuestions.stem: The bill shows a large charge for data transfer between regions. What's the usual fix?
choices: Keep services and the data they read in the same region (or cache close to them), and move cross-region traffic only where needed
why: Cross-region transfer is billed per gigabyte; co-locating removes it.
Commitments don't cover transfer.
Small effect on transfer between services.
Unrelated.

newQuestions.stem: Asked 'users say the site is slow', what's the strongest first move?
choices: Clarify scope and timing (all users? since when? any recent change?), then check user-facing metrics before diving into a server
SSH into a random server and run top
why: Scope and recent changes narrow the search fastest.
A random host may not be involved.
That destroys evidence and may not help.
A guess without evidence.

newQuestions.stem: In an infrastructure design round, the interviewer asks why you chose Kubernetes for a single small web app. What's a strong answer?
choices: Weigh it honestly: a managed container service or platform may be simpler at this size; choose Kubernetes only if there's a reason (many services coming, team skills)
why: They want trade-off reasoning, including when not to use a tool.
Not true.
Not a reason.
Justifying choices is the round.

newQuestions.stem: You're paged: error rates are high and a deploy went out 20 minutes ago. You're not sure the deploy is the cause. What's a sound first action?
choices: Acknowledge, check the dashboards, and, if errors began at the deploy, roll it back as a reversible first step while you keep investigating
Wait an hour to be sure
Turn off monitoring to stop the pages
why: A reversible rollback limits harm while evidence is gathered.
Users suffer meanwhile.
Not at 3 a.m. in an incident.
That hides the problem.
